articles.title: Mossback's Northwest: The Great Wedding Scandal of 1909
articles.author: Knute Berger
paras: It started with an engagement announcement in early March of 1909. The bride was the daughter of the Archdeacon of the Episcopal Church of California whose family lived in Corte Madera in Marin County at a family home called “Daisy Grange.” What made big news was this: the prospective groom was a young Japanese man who was a member of the archdeacon’s household, and the bride-to-be a young, blue-eyed white woman—“the fair picture of girlish innocence,” one newspaper wrote.

What wouldn’t be unusual today was scandalous in California where anti-Asian sentiment was strong. The daughter of an archdeacon marrying a supposed “houseboy” was scandalous on its own, but such interracial marriages were also barred by law in the state. Could their love overcome the marriage ban, social stigma, and an eruption of race hatred? They were about to find out.

The groom-to-be was Gunjiro Aoki, a young man said to be in his mid-20s. His fiancé was Helen Gladys Emery, aged 21. Gunjiro was living in the archdeacon’s home to enhance his Christian education. His elder brother was a pastor at an Episcopal mission for Japanese in San Francisco. It was said Gunjiro’s family traced its line to a noble one of ancient samurai. The two fell in love. Helen’s father, John Emery, disapproved, but her mother Sophronia Frances Emery supported the proposed union, creating a family rift. Aoki’s family wasn’t thrilled about the engagement either.

The couple’s declaration of love and intent to marry caused an out-pouring of threats and hatred that made headlines up and down the West Coast and beyond. It drove intense scrutiny that put the couple’s safety in question.

An angry local mob greeted Helen and her mother at the Corte Madera train station where Helen was subjected to angry women hurling abuse, rice, and calla lilies. Gunjiro Aoki, traveling separately, had bricks thrown at him when he left town along with threats of being tarred and feathered. The Oakland Tribune reported a friend of the Emery’s saying of Helen and her mom, “I believe the mother and girl must be demented, as she sanctions the marriage of her daughter to a Mongolian despite the wishes of her husband and many friends.”

Mrs. Emery fired back: “We are minding our own business, and I wish that others would do the same. Mr. Aoki is a Christian and a gentleman and my daughter loves him….I think the attitude of the people of California in Japanese matters is a disgrace.”

And it wasn’t just in California. Oregon, Idaho, Montana, Nevada and Wyoming all had laws against interracial marriages like this one. The only real option was to find a state that would allow them to wed.

The closest was Washington which, since the late 1860s, had no racial marriage restrictions. They had been eliminated in the Reconstruction era to align with new Constitutional guarantees. But the law was only part of the problem. Civil and church officials often found ways to discourage or deny such unions by questioning the ID of marriage applicants and their witnesses. Many churches and some judges refused to sanction interracial alliances, despite the lack of a legal prohibition.

And there was public approbation. In the press, the Aoki and Emery union was portrayed in racially charged ways. Helen was sometimes referred to as being a “child,” Gunjiro as a scheming “Oriental" who lied about his background, a servant who had seduced a young girl. There were also claims that Helen had been hypnotized into the engagement. That it could be a genuine love match was largely dismissed.

Helen didn’t care even if Gunjiro had a sketchy past as a ne’er do well and womanizer as was claimed by some members of the Japanese community. In a personal letter to Gunjiro published in the San Francisco Examiner, she wrote “Oh, my sweetheart, mother and I could be so happy with you, even in only one room and eating nothing but bread and water….” She signed the letter “Your loving Miko San.”

So, the couple headed to Washington, but threats continued. They were warned not to try marrying in Oregon where another mixed race couple had been driven out of town under threat of arrest as “vagrants.” In Vancouver, WA, the city attorney dared them to try getting married there saying he would do all he could to prevent the union. A rough greeting was expected if they stopped in Tacoma. The couple traveled separately to avoid attention, Helen with her mother. Helen’s father came too by himself, still opposed but resigned. If they were to be married, he wanted it done in his denomination’s church.

Not everyone in Seattle was sympathetic. The Rev. Mark Matthews of the First Presbyterian Church, one of the city’s best-known clergymen and a leading progressive, announced his opposition in the Seattle Times: “My belief is that no Anglo-Saxon girl should be allowed to wed a man of an alien race nor am I in favor of any marriage between whites and those of different races….There should be a law against it.” The Times also painted Archdeacon Emery as the victim with the frontpage headline “Girl’s love of Oriental wrecks home of her father.”

Once in Seattle they got their wedding license and on March 27 they were wed in a quick ceremony at Trinity Episcopal Church on First Hill by the church’s rector Rev. Herbert Henry Gowen, a Japan scholar who had been a missionary in Asia and that year founded the Department of Oriental Studies at the University of Washington, now morphed into the Jackson School of International Studies.

Their marriage did have costs beyond the trauma of racism. Helen lost her American citizenship. After the brief ceremony, John Emery returned alone to California, estranged from his wife and daughter. He resigned his position with the church. Aoki’s brother was forced to quit the mission he’d founded. In the meantime, legislators in Olympia proposed new laws against mixed marriages. They failed.

The couple and Helen’s mother retreated to the rural Eastside of Lake Washington to escape the storm of publicity in hopes of regaining privacy and a new start. The area they chose was no stranger to such marriages. Spurred by the Aoki-Emery union, the Times wrote a story a few months later about a “Lake Washington colony” that it called a “practical experiment in mingling Oriental and Occidental races.”

Newspapers continued speculate about whether and when they would divorce or separate. The couple did move back to California and eventually had four children. Archdeacon Emery and his wife divorced. Mrs. Emery continued to live with her daughter and son-in-law.

They remained married until Gunjiro’s death in 1932 but are said to have led separate lives in later years. Helen changed her last name to Oakie—a name not so Asian sounding—then remarried and the family was said to have lived as “whites.” Helen got her American citizenship back in 1933. She died in 1947.

The trauma of their engagement and marriage made life difficult, excruciating under such a public and hateful lens. But Helen and Gunjiro fought for their right to follow their hearts just like everyone else--whatever the outcome.

articles.title: ‘Mom encouraged me to get breast implants’: Disney child star Christy Carlson Romano on fame, family and freedom
articles.author: Emine Saner
paras: She started acting at six and by 16 was starring in Even Stevens with Shia LaBeouf. Then her career fell apart. Here, she explains how she survived growing up in the spotlight

In a class at college, Christy Carlson Romano was encouraged to think about her “community”. Who were their people, the tutor asked the class, and where did they belong? The answer that popped into Carlson Romano’s head was child actors, but not the ones that went on to have successful grown-up careers. “The ones who were once the shining stars,” she writes in her memoir, “and who are now just trying to find out their places in the world.” Carlson Romano had returned to college after initially dropping out. She had survived sexual assault and toxic relationships, was broke and drinking too much. But before all that, she had been a teenage Disney star. She had made it.

The title of her memoir, Once Upon a Trainwreck, gives you a flavour of where Carlson Romano, 42, is coming from, but what’s most striking isn’t that she goes off the rails (she doesn’t, hugely, compared to other former child stars), but how sensible and mature she is as a child. It’s alarming. When fans recognise her now – she was in the popular Disney series Even Stevens which started in 2000 – they tell her she was a huge part of their childhoods. She had been acting the part of a normal suburban girl, the perfectionist Ren Stevens, while having no idea what that was like. She was already a mini adult.

articles.title: Pope Leo’s trip is a homecoming to Peru – where debate over liberation theology roiled the church during his early years as a priest
articles.author:
<name>Eben Levey, Assistant Professor of History, Rochester Institute of Technology</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/eben-levey-1510559"/>
paras: Pope Leo XIV travels to Latin America on Nov. 6, 2026, with a packed itinerary that will bring him through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It is Leo’s first trip to the region since his elevation to the papacy – and a homecoming for a pope who spent two decades in Peru and holds Peruvian citizenship.
As a historian of Catholicism in the late 20th century , I couldn’t help but notice that the pope’s plans walk a fine line during a fraught political moment in Latin America.

Leo plans to meet with the right-wing presidents of Argentina and Peru . He will also visit sites often associated with the progressive wing of the Catholic Church, including Casavalle, one of the poorest neighborhoods in Uruguay’s capital. In Argentina, where President Javier Milei has drastically cut funding for disability services, the pope will go to a Catholic home for disabled people.

And in Chiclayo, Peru, where Leo served as a bishop, he will pray at a chapel dedicated to St. Óscar Romero. A Salvadoran archbishop, Romero was assassinated in 1980 after years of speaking out against the human rights violations committed by the U.S.-supported Salvadoran military . His ministry was influenced by liberation theology , a controversial movement born in Peru that roiled church politics for decades – including during Leo’s years in Peru.
The name itself was coined in a 1968 lecture by Gustavo Gutiérrez , a Peruvian theologian and priest. He expanded on his ideas in a 1971 book, “ A Theology of Liberation .”

Gutiérrez and like-minded theologians argued that Christians have a moral duty to liberate the oppressed . They saw poverty, violence, racism and discrimination as not just problems but collective sins. While building on earlier Catholic social teachings, these “liberationists” envisioned profound change that went beyond the spiritual care and charitable work of traditional Latin American Catholicism.

Catholics inspired by liberation theology created community organizations and work cooperatives, organized labor unions and fostered other initiatives that sought to measurably improve the lives of the poor. In my own research , I’ve documented how priests and nuns in rural Mexico helped organize transportation, corn milling and carpentry cooperatives.

Gutiérrez also argued that Christians should use Marxist ideas about analyzing society and the economy to better understand inequality . In nations like Peru, which possessed rich natural resources , liberationists tailored their economic justice projects to address how international and national companies profited off the low wages of miners and farmers.
During the Cold War, however, these ideas led some politicians and church leaders to accuse liberationists of socialism and communism.

A minority fringe of liberationists did embrace left-ring radicalism. Christians for Socialism , for example, argued that liberation meant rejecting capitalism . Some clergy, although only a handful, even picked up arms to fight alongside clandestine left-wing revolutionary groups.

In 1891, Pope Leo XIII – the current pope’s namesake – published “Rerum Novarum ,” an encyclical focused on workers’ rights amid the Industrial Revolution. Since then, the Vatican had critiqued the worst excesses of capitalism while also rejecting socialism and communism, which it viewed as godless ideologies.

During the 1960s and ’70s, Pope Paul VI generally supported local initiatives by liberationist Catholics , including some in Chulucanas, Peru , where Leo began his missionary work. Paul appointed and elevated bishops who shared a vision that the church could help empower the poor and alleviate oppression.

But the Vatican shifted when the Polish cardinal Karol Józef Wojtyla became Pope John Paul II in 1978. For most of his adult life, Poland had been part of the Soviet bloc, which imposed restrictions on organized religion. A staunch opponent of communism , he worried about liberation theology’s use of Marxist analysis. So did one of his top Vatican officials, Joseph Ratzinger – the future Pope Benedict XVI.

The Vatican began investigating some liberation theologians for violations of church teachings. In 1985, for example, Brazilian liberationist theologian Leonardo Boff was ordered to observe a year of silence – no publishing, no public speaking – to discipline him for his critique of the church’s hierarchy. Several priests were suspended over their work in Sandinista Nicaragua.
John Paul ordered that the Peruvian bishops begin an investigation of Gutiérrez – above all, over Marxism’s influence on his work . Gutiérrez was ultimately not punished.

One factor in his favor may have been his consistent opposition to armed revolution, even before violence raged in Peru from the 1980s into the ’90s. The Shining Path , a Maoist guerrilla group, was waging a war of terrorism against the Peruvian government, setting off bombs across Peru.

Under President Alberto Fujimori, the government escalated existing counterinsurgency operations, often using indiscriminate violence against citizens in the region where the Shining Path emerged. In 2009, Fujimori was convicted of human rights violations .

Leo has never described himself as a liberationist Catholic. However, his experiences as a priest were indelibly shaped by liberation theology , the Peruvian armed conflict and the church debates that roiled much of Latin America during his years there.

Leo, born Robert Prevost, was raised in Chicago. After ordination, his journey as a priest began in Peru, where he landed for missionary work in 1985. The young friar followed in the footsteps of other U.S. Catholic missionaries who had been serving among Peru’s poor and Indigenous, urban and rural, since the 1940s.

Sent to Chulucanas, in Peru’s coastal northwest, Prevost found himself in a region of pastoral experimentation. Since the 1960s, Augustinian missionaries had been working closely with the community to provide literacy education, discussion groups about poverty and inequality, and workshops to train artisans.

These programs were a far cry from the more radical actions of some Catholics who supported liberation theology. Nevertheless, the programs in Chulucanas aimed to empower the Peruvian poor, chipping away at exploitation and low wages on the region’s sugarcane and cotton estates. Like Gutiérrez, many Peruvian Christians believed that the Shining Path drew support because of pervasive poverty and inequality , and that churches could help transform the nation.

But the Catholic Church in Latin America was in the midst of another transformation. John Paul gradually appointed conservative bishops across the continent. Experimental pastoral programs lost support, and institutions that trained priests to put liberation theology into action, such as the Regional Seminary of the Southeast in Mexico, were shuttered or “reoriented.”

Yet even as the hierarchy shifted conservative, work on the ground among Latin America’s poorest continued apace. From coffee cooperatives in Mexico to human rights activists across the continent, many programs survived.

Leo’s 2026 itinerary includes multiple stops that speak to this history and on-the-ground pastoral work. The most symbolic, perhaps, is the Capilla San Óscar Romero, located in Chiclayo, the pope’s former diocese.

A neighborhood chapel renovated with donations from Leo’s connections in the United States, it is one of many sites throughout the Americas honoring Catholics who fell victim to right-wing, anti-communist violence. The day before Romero’s assassination, he used his weekly radio address to speak directly to El Salvador’s conscripted soldiers, telling them, “ No soldier is obliged to obey an order counter to the law of God .”

Leo XIV’s visit to the chapel is for private prayer, not a homily or a speech. Still, I would argue that the soft-spoken pope’s stop will evoke Romero’s message – especially at a time of strikes against suspected drug traffickers , which human rights groups have criticized as extrajudicial killings . During his final Mass , Romero pleaded, “I beseech you, I beg you, I command you in the name of God: Cease the repression!”

articles.title: Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms stands on the shoulders of Stacey Abrams, Charlotta Bass and countless other Black women who dreamed
articles.author:
<name>Allissa V. Richardson, Associate Professor of Journalism, USC Annenberg School for Communication and Journalism</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/allissa-v-richardson-1068279"/>
paras: There are elections that change the political map. And then there are elections that make you wonder whether the land itself remembers.
The auction blocks . The cotton fields . The lynching trees . The Black women who cleaned governors’ homes but could not dream of becoming governor themselves.
And now Keisha Lance Bottoms has been elected Georgia’s first Black woman governor . The first Black woman elected governor of any American state.
Bottoms has traced her ancestry back five generations to an enslaved person on a plantation near Crawfordville, Georgia.
An ancestor held in bondage on Georgia soil. A descendant elected to govern it.
The same earth. An entirely different claim to power. How many women had to believe in a future they would never live to see?

Bottoms’s victory represents the paradox of Black political advancement amid racial violence and the often-unrecognized labor of women who build futures they may never inhabit. Ultimately, Bottoms’ victory reflects both extraordinary progress and the unfinished work of American democracy.
I keep thinking about the little children.

Between 1979 and 1981, Atlanta was terrorized by the disappearances and murders of Black children and young adults. Mothers pleaded for answers. Families lived in a city where childhood itself had become dangerous.

The murders unfolded just years after Maynard Jackson’s historic 1973 election as Atlanta’s first Black mayor. His victory announced a new era of Black political power. Yet that power could not shield the city’s most vulnerable children. Suspicions of Ku Klux Klan involvement circulated , although the Klan’s responsibility was never established.
That distinction matters. So does the fear.

Bottoms was born in 1970 . She was 9 when the murders began. She grew up in the same Atlanta where Black parents searched desperately for their missing children. She belonged to the generation whose futures were being stolen. And now she is preparing to lead the entire state.
What a terrible, beautiful, complicated thing.
Those murdered children were not symbols waiting to become useful to history. They were sons and daughters who deserved the ordinary miracle of growing older. They deserved a future.

Bottoms later occupied the mayor’s office that Jackson first opened to Black leadership. Now she is preparing to occupy the governor’s mansion. History has not erased its cruelty. But it has delivered an astonishing answer.
And this victory does not belong to Bottoms alone.
This victory belongs, in no small measure, to democracy advocate, legislator and lawyer Stacey Abrams . Perhaps those who recognize what Abrams made possible have sent her flowers.

Abrams ran for Georgia governor in 2018 and 2022. She lost both races . But through the New Georgia Project and Fair Fight , organizations focused on engaging voters and protecting voting rights, she helped build an electorate that could imagine Georgia differently. She registered voters, challenged barriers to participation , and refused to accept that the South’s political future was fixed.

And now another Black woman has won the office Abrams twice sought, in the third gubernatorial race in a row headed by a Black Democratic woman . There is something biblical about the path Abrams steadfastly cleared. I think of Moses, guiding his people toward the Promised Land but never entering it himself.

Abrams’ journey is not over. Nor should her accomplishments be measured by another woman’s victory. But I believe there is sacred work in preparing a future you may never personally enjoy. Some people plant trees. Some people sit in their shade. Stacey Abrams planted. Bottoms is standing beneath the branches.
And as a scholar of Black media history , I can reach even further back, to another woman who understood the audacity of claiming political power: Charlotta Bass .
In 1952, Bass became the first Black woman nominated for vice president of the United States, running on the Progressive Party ticket.
Before the Voting Rights Act in 1965, before the March on Washington in 1963, before Jackson was elected mayor in 1973 and before Abrams or Bottoms drew their first breaths, there was Bass.

A Black newspaper publisher who confronted segregation, police brutality and white supremacist violence in her four-decade ownership of The California Eagle , Bass understood that political power was about more than winning office. It was about who had the right to imagine themselves in one.

Bass ran when a Black woman entering the White House seemed almost unimaginable. Almost. But not to her. I imagine she would have loved this election. And I suspect she would have had pointed questions for Gov.-elect Bottoms.
What will you do for the poor? The disenfranchised? How will you protect the vote that brought you here?

History-making is not the same as justice-making, and representation matters. The true measure of Bottoms’ victory will be whether Georgians experience the more just state she promised to bring about .

For generations, Black women have been asked to save a democracy that would not save them. We have carried clipboards, protest signs and entire movements on our backs. We have been told to wait. To be patient. To be grateful.
And now a Black woman has been elected to govern Georgia.

The children have not returned. The past has not been undone. But something has shifted. Charlotta dreamed it. Stacey helped build it. Keisha has won it. And somewhere, another little Black girl is watching. She may not understand the history. She may only know that the governor-elect looks like her. For now, that is enough to begin a dream.
And history has taught us what can happen when a Black girl begins to dream.

articles.title: Young people turned out in near-record numbers for the 2026 midterms, with the economy top of their minds
articles.author:
<name>Sara Suzuki, Senior Researcher and Research Assistant Professor at CIRCLE, Tufts University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/sara-suzuki-2776180"/>
paras: The economy was the top issue for voters in the November 2026 midterm elections, which saw Democrats win decisive majorities in both houses of Congress.

And for young voters, whether in college or not, the economy and jobs, as well as healthcare, were their top concerns, our research at CIRCLE , a nonpartisan, research organization focused on youth civic engagement at Tufts University, shows.

Overall, 27% of young people – meaning people ages 18 to 29 – went to the polls during the midterms, our Nov. 5 analysis shows. This marks the second-highest midterm youth voter turnout in the past 30 years, behind only the 2018 election cycle.

As a scholar at CIRCLE who studies young people and their voting behavior, I think it’s helpful to understand some of the factors that motivated so many young people to vote – and to cast their lot with the Democrats.
Among youth, being enrolled as a college student or not did not make a big difference in who they voted for during these midterms.

But there are some voting trend differences based on young people’s educational attainment, especially in the gap between young people with an education level of high school or less, and those with at least some college experience and more. Those with only a high school degree or less voted Democratic by a 24-point margin, compared with a 42-point margin among those with at least some college education.

College students who are young men also voted Democrat by a 24-point margin . Female college students, meanwhile, voted Democrat at a 45-point margin. A similar gender gap appears among young voters who aren’t in college.
Overall, this gender gap has persisted at least since 2024, as young women then were also voting more Democratic than men were.

About 66% of young people ages 18-29 voted for a Democratic candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives, compared with 31% for a Republican candidate, our data shows. This marks the highest percentage of support for Democratic candidates among all age groups.
Within this group, 70% of young women voted for a Democratic U.S. House candidate in the midterms, as opposed to 59% of young men.
Partisan trends among young voters have fluctuated over the past few decades – in 2000, for example, 49% of young people voted Democratic, while 48% voted Republican.

In 2026, Asian American and Pacific Islander, Black and Latino young people gave Democrat candidates the strongest support, at 81%, 79% and 71%, respectively. By comparison, 61% of white young people voted for Democratic House candidates, with 36% voting Republican.
Across race, education, income and geographic location, young people overwhelmingly indicated that the economy and jobs was their top issue in this election.
Healthcare and the Iran war also showed up as areas of importance for young voters. All three of these issues are connected to young people’s concerns about the cost of living.
We found that voting preferences did vary according to how young people viewed their own financial circumstances, a pattern that held among college students.
Low-income students were more likely than their affluent peers to vote for Democrats .
The issues that matter most to young people have shifted considerably over the past several years.
In 2020, we were seeing different groups of young people prioritize social issues like racism , climate change and gun control.
In 2022, we began to see young people prioritize the economy – their concern about inflation was the second-most important issue to them after abortion.

Now, after the economy , healthcare was ranked second for young voters. The third-most important issue was the war in Iran. This is striking, because in the past, we’ve polled young voters about foreign policy issues like the war between Israel and Palestinians and the war between Russia and Ukraine. Young people have never really ranked these other foreign policy issues as a top area of concern.

Youth voter turnout generally tends to be much weaker in midterm elections than in presidential elections. In 2018, there was 28% turnout for young people – a midterm turnout that was considerably higher than 2014, when only 13% of young people turned out to vote.

Campaigns seem to recognize that young voters tend to be less politically engaged. For example, our research shows that during the 2024 presidential election cycle, more than 1 in 3 young people were never contacted about the election. Among those without college experience, 48% were never contacted.
Our research still shows that college students face logistical barriers to voting.

Young people are frequent movers, which means they might need to reregister whenever they change addresses. The fact that college students may be living on campus while they’re registered to vote from their parents’ address can also create complications.

College students still have more voting information than young people who are not in college. But compared with other age groups, young people receive less voting information – making their turnout in the 2026 midterms all the more remarkable.

articles.title: What C.S. Lewis said about Narnia’s most famous character: the Jesus-like lion Aslan
articles.author:
<name>Christopher A. Snyder, PhD, Professor of History, Mississippi State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/christopher-a-snyder-phd-805968"/>
paras: As Netflix teases glimpses of Greta Gerwig’s newest project , an adaptation of C.S. Lewis’ novel “The Magician’s Nephew,” many Narnia fans are worried . In particular, there’s been online chatter about the new film’s depiction of the great lion Aslan: Will he really look like David Bowie , with the voice of Meryl Streep ?

For many readers, Aslan is not just a literary character, nor an ordinary hero: He is a representation of Jesus . Aslan sings the entire world of Narnia into existence and performs Christ-like acts throughout Lewis’ “ Chronicles of Narnia ,” which have sold over 120 million copies worldwide since the series’ publication in the 1950s.

As a scholar of medieval history and literature, I’ve taught and written about Lewis and “Lord of the Rings” author J.R.R. Tolkien , who were close friends and colleagues for more than 30 years. Lewis himself was a medievalist at Oxford , and both of their popular literary series are steeped in their knowledge of medieval languages, literature, mythology and theology.
Both authors acknowledged the ethical and religious themes of their fiction . Yet Lewis rejected the idea that “The Chronicles” were simply an allegory.

“ The Magician’s Nephew ,” published in 1955, was actually the last book in the series to be completed. Yet it serves as a prequel, narrating the creation of Narnia and the first appearance of its legitimate ruler, Aslan – the Turkish word for “lion.”

Later in the series, Aslan sacrifices himself to save a young British boy, Edmund Pevensie, from the White Witch, Jadis. Aslan is resurrected through his knowledge of “deeper magic,” and royal power passes to the four Pevensie children.

Christian readers have long seen the series as an imaginative retelling of events from the Gospels, intended for children but offering much to adult readers as well. Critics like Philip Pullman , who wrote the 1990s fantasy trilogy “His Dark Materials,” have denounced “The Chronicles” as religious “propaganda .”

Adding to the book’s religious appeal was Lewis’ own very public faith. An atheist since his youth, he returned to worshipping in the Church of England after a famous late-night conversation with Tolkien in September 1931.

The two English professors had bonded over their interest in Norse myths, which Lewis called beautiful “lies breathed through silver.” For the devoutly Catholic Tolkien, however, ancient myths pointed to truths, not lies, and ultimately to the Gospels. He and other Christian friends at Oxford helped Lewis come to accept Christianity as the “true myth.”

Almost immediately, Lewis began writing Christian apologetics , intellectual defenses of his faith, as well as fiction infused with Christian symbolism and theology. In 1947, he appeared on the cover of Time magazine – well on his way to becoming arguably the most famous Christian apologist of the 20th century.
But what did Lewis himself say about Aslan?

His letters and scholarly work indicate that “The Chronicles” were not meant to be allegorical . In other words, Aslan was not simply a stand-in for Jesus, and the series was not an extended metaphor.
Rather, Lewis called the books “supposals:” a way of asking, “What if?”

Aslan gives “an imaginary answer to the question, ‘What might Christ become like if there really were a world like Narnia and He chose to be incarnate and die and rise again in that world as He actually has done in ours?” Lewis wrote in a 1958 letter . “This is not allegory at all.”

Neither Lewis nor Tolkien approved of easy allegorical readings of their fiction. Both professors argued that imaginative literature was not simply the product of the author and their time , a sealed treasure waiting for a biographical key to unlock its meaning.

And both men knew formal allegory quite well. Lewis’ 1936 book “ The Allegory of Love ” established his reputation as a critic of medieval and Renaissance literature. His 1933 novel “ The Pilgrim’s Regress ” was an allegorical exploration of his own conversion, with characters that personified various abstract concepts and ideologies.

Tolkien wrote the allegorical short story “ Leaf by Niggle ” as a way to explore his own doubts about ever finishing “ The Lord of the Rings .” Like his earlier novel “ The Hobbit ,” “The Lord of the Rings” only came to fruition through Lewis’ constant encouragement.

Narnia came to Lewis’ mind in bits and pieces. During World War II, when he took young evacuees from bombed cities into his home, a lion had haunted his dreams. A few other mental pictures came to him – a faun carrying packages, a lamppost in the snow – and he began writing. Aslan “just insisted on behaving in His own way,” Lewis later wrote to one schoolgirl .

“The Chronicles” were not an allegory, he insisted, but symbolic. As he described in “ The Allegory of Love ,” “The symbolist leaves the given [facts] to find that which is more real.” Myth and symbols can, if used correctly, point to philosophical or theological truths more effectively than realistic fiction, making their created worlds feel more real.

For fans of “The Chronicles,” Narnia feels “real” in this sense – an escape to truth, rather than an escape from truth. Adapting these stories to film, however, always runs the risk of moving further away from what Lewis captured so brilliantly in his prose.

In 2018, the author’s estate sold Netflix the rights to adapt the book series to screen, and Gerwig was later tapped to write and direct at least two Narnia films. Douglas Gresham, one of Lewis’ stepsons, has an executive producer credit on “ Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew ,” and has generally been enthusiastic about the project.

Gerwig herself has expressed her “reverence” for Lewis’ work . “It was the book of my childhood,” she said at a press event in 2024. “It was the book series that I loved, and I lived through, and I spent so much time imagining myself inside of Narnia.”

Intense scrutiny of the project should surprise no one. As with her film “Little Women,” Gerwig is adapting a beloved novel . And this time, it is a novel written by a very public atheist-turned-Christian whose works have inspired the faith of countless others. Still, her “Magician’s Nephew” should not be judged by a trailer and a handful of interviews.

Lewis likely never expected that “The Chronicles” would turn into a live-action film, but he did believe in the power of imaginative art – whether ancient, medieval or modern – to move one toward truth. The virtues Faith, Hope, Charity and Prudence are frequently depicted in the medieval and Renaissance literature that Lewis loved and taught. Fans and filmmaker alike might benefit from remembering these virtues as well.

articles.title: I’m an athletic trainer – here’s how to know when kids sports are too intense
articles.author:
<name>Adam Annaccone, Clinical Associate Professor of Kinesiology, University of Texas at Arlington</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/adam-annaccone-2615381"/>
paras: At a recent T-ball game, I was talking with another father who mentioned that his son had never played before. As we watched our children falling over trying to scoop up a ground ball, we laughed about how they were still figuring everything out. There was something refreshing about seeing kids learn a game without worrying about how well they were playing.

That moment stayed with me. I’ve spent years as an athletic trainer in collegiate and professional sports, helping athletes stay healthy, handle the demands of competition and perform at their best. Today, I’m a clinical associate professor of kinesiology and chief health and performance adviser for an NCAA Division I athletics program. Given my work, you might expect me to take an active role in developing my own children’s athletic abilities, especially in a youth sports culture where early specialization and greater commitment are often seen as advantages.

And I understand the appeal. Like any parent, I want my children to have opportunities, and it’s easy to wonder whether another practice or lesson might help them get ahead. But with twins who are nearly 6, I’m more interested in whether they enjoy sports than how good they become at them.

As they get older, particularly if they want to pursue sports seriously, my role as a parent will change. Right now, I can step back and let them explore. But as training and competition become more demanding, I’ll want to become more involved in understanding and questioning those demands. Research on training, recovery and athletic development can help parents navigate what’s appropriate as their children’s sports experiences intensify.

When I’m watching my children play, I’d rather be their dad than their performance coach. When they ask to practice hitting or throwing, I’m happy to help. They usually decide when we’re done. Twenty minutes? Great. Five minutes? That’s fine too.
Practice matters, but giving children some control over when and how they practice can help keep it from becoming another obligation.

Research involving more than 9,000 young athletes found that children tend to be more motivated to participate in sports when parents support their ability to make decisions about their participation .

As children get older, their goals may change. Some will want to compete at higher levels or focus on a particular sport. Those ambitions deserve support, but giving children a voice doesn’t mean parents should step away from important decisions. As commitments grow, parents may need to ask more questions about training schedules, recovery time and the expectations placed on their children.

I’ve heard parents describe traveling hours for youth sports tournaments, only to discover that many of the teams competing came from the same communities they had traveled from. One parent recalled driving to Houston for a tournament where six of the eight teams were from the Dallas-Fort Worth area.

I understand how families end up in these situations. An extra practice, private lessons or joining a more competitive team can each seem reasonable. Over time, those commitments become expectations, and saying no isn’t always easy when your child is part of a team.

But more training doesn’t automatically produce better athletes. My experience in sports medicine and performance has taught me that improvement depends on how athletes respond to training, not simply how much they do. Training places demands on the body , and athletes need time to adapt.

The American Academy of Pediatrics cautions that excessive training and early specialization are associated with increased overuse injury risk and may contribute to burnout. Risk depends on training volume, recovery and individual development, particularly during adolescence.

As training demands increase, parents should pay attention to how their children are responding, not just whether they’re experiencing pain. Persistent fatigue, declining performance, changes in sleep or a loss of enthusiasm may suggest that recovery isn’t keeping pace with training. Even an athlete who loves their sport can reach a point where the demands become too much. These are reasons for a parent to discuss the workload with their child and coaches, while persistent or worsening pain warrants medical evaluation.

Athletic development also benefits from variety. Running, climbing, jumping and exploring different activities can help develop coordination and a range of movement skills . The International Olympic Committee recommends varied physical activity and developmentally appropriate training, including for children who may eventually specialize.

Just as important is whether young athletes want to keep playing. Children who enjoy sports are more likely to want to continue participating , research shows. When young soccer players were asked what made sports fun , they identified working hard, improving and spending time with teammates. Even the best training program won’t accomplish much if an athlete no longer wants to participate.

In collegiate and professional sports, reviewing performance is routine. After competition, staff identify what worked, what didn’t and what needs attention. But children don’t need a performance review every time they climb into the car.

I let my children start conversations about their games. If they want to talk about a missed ball, something funny or something that upset them, I’ll listen. If they want to talk about something else, that’s fine too.

Researchers who recorded parent-child car rides around sporting events found that much of the time passed in silence and sports came up relatively infrequently . They also observed occasions when parents interrupted or provided feedback before children could respond. The findings don’t establish one right way to handle the drive home, but they offer parents a reason to consider whether their children want feedback in the first place.

No parent knows whether their child will become a competitive athlete, play recreationally or eventually find interests outside organized sports. I’m comfortable leaving that future open for my children. As a father, I’m far more interested in whether my kids will want to play again next week than how well they played today.

articles.title: What the measles vaccine’s ‘97% effective’ rating means for Pittsburgh parents
articles.author:
<name>Rebecca Smullin Dawson, Associate Professor of Biology, Allegheny College</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/rebecca-smullin-dawson-1436960"/>
paras: Pennsylvania is experiencing its worst measles outbreak in more than three decades, with more than 1,400 confirmed cases and six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, according to statistics compiled by the state.

Each new case brings a new warning of a measles exposure in that community. Exposures have occurred at hospitals and doctors’ offices , grocery stores and restaurants , and K-12 schools and universities .

Exposure alerts come with the same instructions: Check your MMR vaccine status, and watch for symptoms for the next three weeks. People are told that two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are 97% effective at preventing measles. The underlying message is that if you’re vaccinated, you’re protected.
The MMR vaccine is highly effective at preventing disease, but it isn’t a guarantee. People may hear that 97% figure and wonder about the other 3% .

Parents ask me: Should I be worried? How do I know if my kid has measles? Do I need an MMR booster? Most recently, my teenage daughter texted me to ask about her MMR vaccine status. She was worried about what would happen if she were exposed.

These are questions I can answer as both a mother and an epidemiologist in northwestern Pennsylvania . I became both at once. My daughter was born at the start of my doctoral program, and I read epidemiology textbooks aloud to her while studying for my comprehensive exams. I defended my dissertation on my son’s due date. I’m a better mother because I’m an epidemiologist, and a better epidemiologist because I’m a mom.
The advice in each public measles exposure alert matches the guidance doctors follow when a patient may have been exposed.

Everyone is asked to watch for symptoms , whether or not they’re vaccinated. The number of unvaccinated people across Pennsylvania is growing . As a result, many communities , including Allegheny County, no longer have herd immunity.
Four of the over 1,400 confirmed measles cases in Pennsylvania were people who had been vaccinated . These cases are known as breakthrough infections .

The term “herd immunity” wasn’t coined until 1918 . That year, a veterinarian wrote about an outbreak of “contagious abortion” in sheep and cattle, a literal herd. Today, herd immunity means that the risk of disease for susceptible people, those without immunity, drops when they are surrounded by people who are immune.

In other words, if the people around you are immune, you’re unlikely to get sick even if you’re susceptible. For measles, that protection depends on about 95% of people being immune. In a school or community where fewer than 95% of people are vaccinated, measles can spread more easily.
In Allegheny County, 93.8% of children are fully vaccinated against measles . Some neighborhoods are above 97% uptake, while others are below the necessary 95% needed for herd immunity .

Measles exposures are announced publicly by the Department of Health and local healthcare providers . During a measles outbreak, public health departments may get in touch with close contacts to alert them to an exposure.

Public exposure alerts, like the one made in October after there was a measles exposure at a Target near Pittsburgh , are also used. Public alerts are for settings where exposed people can’t be identified and contacted individually. Measles is so contagious that a single case can infect up to 18 susceptible people .
Measles spreads through the air and through respiratory droplets, like those released when someone sneezes. The virus can also survive outside the body , lingering in the air and on surfaces.

Imagine I have measles and walk into my local grocery store. I’m contagious from about four days before the rash appears until four days after. Every time I breathe out, I release virus particles into the air, and those particles can stay infectious for up to two hours. If I sneeze in the produce section, the virus can survive on surfaces for up to two hours.

However, if you’ve had measles or were vaccinated with two doses of the MMR vaccine, you are protected. Two doses provides 97% lifetime protection against measles . This means that even without herd immunity, fewer than 3% of individuals with immunity are likely to contract measles. Adults who have had measles, or who have documentation of the recommended doses of the MMR vaccine, don’t need a booster .

People who were vaccinated between 1963 and 1967, or who aren’t sure which vaccine they received, should talk to their primary care provider about whether they need another dose. This is because the measles vaccine used between those years was not as effective as the MMR vaccine that is currently given .

Today, children typically get their first dose of the MMR vaccine at 12 to 15 months old and a second dose at 4 to 6 years old . Because the vaccine is given in early childhood, people born in the early to mid-1960s are the most likely to have received the older vaccine. People born before 1957 are generally considered immune , because measles was so widespread then that almost everyone caught it as a child.

Symptoms of measles include a high fever that can reach 105 degrees Fahrenheit (40.6 degrees Celsius), a cough, a runny nose and conjunctivitis, also known as pin keye. These symptoms overlap with those of other respiratory viruses, such as flu and COVID-19.

Most people with measles develop a red, blotchy rash. It starts on the face and spreads down the body, like paint poured from a bucket . People who are immunocompromised or were previously vaccinated, even with one dose of the MMR vaccine, may not develop the rash. Between 25% and 40% of immunocompromised people with measles never get the rash .
A telltale sign of measles is Koplik spots , tiny white spots inside the mouth that can show up a day or two before the rash.

Measles can have serious consequences. About 1 in 20 people with measles develop pneumonia, and up to 3 in 1,000 cases end in death. Children younger than 5 and adults older than 20 are most likely to experience these severe complications.

Without herd immunity in many communities, measles cases, hospitalizations and deaths in Pennsylvania are likely to keep rising. The state Department of Health reports community spread of measles in 14 of Pennsylvania’s 67 counties .

Each of these cases is mostly preventable with the MMR vaccine. The U.S. declared measles eliminated in 2000 , meaning it was no longer spreading continuously here. This year’s outbreak shows how quickly that can change and the negative health consequences it can have in our communities.
Read more of our stories about Pittsburgh and Pennsylvania .
