articles.title: Seattle startup OneCourt brings tactile tablets for blind and low-vision fans to NHL games
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Seattle startup OneCourt is bringing its haptic devices for blind and low-vision sports fans to hockey, with the NHL and Ticketmaster making the tablets available free at the league’s marquee events this season and at all home games for four teams.
The device turns real-time game data into vibrations that users follow with their fingertips. For hockey, OneCourt draws on the NHL’s EDGE puck and player tracking data.
The tablets debuted at the Heritage Classic on Oct. 25, and the Washington Capitals, Colorado Avalanche, Chicago Blackhawks and Detroit Red Wings are the first clubs to offer them at every home game.
“Our community has been asking us for hockey since day one, and launching it with Ticketmaster and the NHL is a milestone for OneCourt,” CEO Jerred Mace said in a news release.

The hockey launch builds on OneCourt’s work in other leagues, starting with the NBA’s Portland Trail Blazers. Since 2025, Ticketmaster has offered the tablets at every home game for nine NBA teams, and it backed an NFL pilot during the 2025 season with four clubs, including the Seattle Seahawks , along with Super Bowl LX.

Mace started OneCourt as a University of Washington student studying industrial and product design. His co-founders are three fellow UW grads: COO Antyush Bollini, CTO Andrew Buckingham and CIO Nick Durand.
Time named OneCourt’s tablet to its Best Inventions of 2026 list last month, in the accessibility category. It was one of several Seattle-area innovations on the list.

articles.title: Seattle Police Department Enjoys Unique Privileges, Insulation from Accountability
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: Seattle’s public safety departments – particularly the Seattle Police Department (SPD) – have historically received unique treatment and favored allocation of resources, including both money and technological tools. Reviewing recent developments in the City of Seattle, that special treatment does not look to disappear any time soon.

Until it was terminated after 15 years by Judge James Robart last fall, SPD’s consent decree acted as a reminder of the impunity under which SPD had routinely been allowed to operate. The dismissal of the consent decree was postponed after SPD officers responded to the George Floyd protests of 2020 with violence and the indiscriminate use of less lethal weapons such as tear gas, pepper spray, and rubber bullets.

In the final consent decree hearing , Robart repeatedly talked about how the Seattle Police Officers Guild (SPOG) contract had “neutered” Seattle’s police accountability ordinance. While utilization of the Community Assisted Response and Engagement (CARE) team has recently improved following the departure of former SPD Chief Shon Barnes, the SPOG contract has also hampered the CARE team’s ability to respond to appropriate calls.

SPD receives a large share of the City’s discretionary General Fund. Public safety as a whole accounts for 53% of the $2 billion of General Fund expenditures in Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson’s proposed 2027 budget, and by itself, SPD receives more than a quarter of the total General Fund.

That largesse comes in spite of the lack of fiscal responsibility demonstrated by the department. One recent example: in June of this year, SPD overpaid about 900 of their employees by $13.1 million due to a “payroll error.” Because most of these employees are represented by SPOG, the City will have to negotiate with SPOG to try to recover the bulk of these funds, meaning it could be years before the money returns to the City’s coffers.

Four and a half months after the error, neither the Mayor’s Office nor SPD would comment about whether they have identified the person or persons responsible for this mistake or whether any disciplinary action would be taken.

In addition, neither the Mayor’s Office nor SPD shared any plans to avoid such errors in the future. While the overpayment was one time in nature since it was caused by an error in the calculation of payment of retroactive pay increases provided by recent union contracts, it could presumably be made again the next time new contracts require a similar calculation.

SPD receives special budgetary consideration beyond the mere size of its annual budget in the way the department routinely overspends its overtime budget. Data from a council central staff report in 2015 showed that SPD had overspent its overtime all but one year from 1995-2014, a trend that has continued, including this year and last year .

SPD has also traditionally received an extra slush fund through “ghost cop” positions , funded officer positions that will definitely not be filled. While these positions have finally been eliminated, under the current 2027 budget proposal, SPD is expected to achieve $4.5 million in salary savings.

The Seattle Fire Department (SFD) might also get in on the slush fund act. SFD took a cut to its overtime budget in Wilson’s proposed 2027-2028 budget, with two competing budget amendments from councilmembers looking to address this cut. Budget Chair Dan Strauss and Councilmember Maritza Rivera had identical amendments proposing to restore SFD’s overtime by the full $7.1 million amount of the cut.

Councilmember Dionne Foster’s amendment, on the other hand, suggested increasing SFD’s overtime by $5.1 million. Foster had asked council’s central staff to do an analysis to come up with this number based on the number of new hires at SFD, as well as the likelihood that some shifts at SFD would remain uncovered due to lack of volunteers to do overtime. Foster’s goal was to achieve the same target daily staffing level with fewer dollars.

“If SFD does receive this $7.1 million in overtime funding, but does not spend it all for that purpose, that funding will be in the SFD budget, and it will be available to cover unbudgeted costs in other areas,” said Ann Gorman, a central staff analyst. “Perhaps SFD will need funding in some other areas that haven’t been identified, and unneeded overtime costs will just be shifted into those accounts.”

Budget Chair Dan Strauss chose to include the larger $7.1 million SFD overtime addition to his balancing package released this week, potentially allowing SFD access to $2 million they are unlikely to use for overtime.

SPD got into hot water back in 2012 when the Seattle City Council learned that the department had obtained two unmanned aerial drones via a federal homeland security grant they received in 2010. SPD hadn’t kept the council informed about their plans to use the drones even though they’d already started training officers in their usage. At that time, the department hadn’t drafted any policies around usage of the drones. A public outcry led to the SPD abandoning their drone plans, and the ACLU took the opportunity to ask the City for a surveillance ordinance.

A surveillance equipment ordinance was passed in 2013 , but that wasn’t the end of the saga. Instead, SPD secretly purchased social media tracking software in 2014, which, when discovered in 2016, the department said wasn’t covered under the surveillance equipment ordinance because it was software, not hardware. This episode ultimately led to the council passing a new, revamped surveillance ordinance in 2017 .

More recently, two audits released earlier this year showed further overreach on SPD’s part. In the last year, SPD integrated several unapproved Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) traffic camera feeds into its real-time crime center. While SPD failed to adopt a formal policy around how it would integrate private cameras into its real-time crime center, the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) also found SPD has trouble following its own camera masking requirements for private areas viewed by its cameras due to the lack of availability of technicians.
Now questions have arisen about SPD’s usage of aerial drones, which originally led to Seattle having a surveillance ordinance and is still not allowed.
However, the King County Sheriff's Office (KCSO) has a fleet of drones that can fly into Seattle to help SPD, whether that be for large events like World Cup games or after emergencies.

“We have concerns that KCSO drones flying over Seattle enables SPD to essentially bypass the Seattle surveillance ordinance and the protections it is intended to provide,” said Tee Sannon, ACLU-WA’s technology policy program director. “Without proper regulation, drones pose a serious threat to people's privacy and civil liberties. They can carry multiple surveillance tools that capture data about people and their movements without their knowledge or consent, which could potentially chill free speech and impinge on people's free association rights. For law enforcement agencies seeking to use tools like drones, the use must be carefully regulated to minimize these threats from surveillance, such as by placing strict limits on what data they can collect, how long it can be retained, how it can be used, and who it can be shared with.”

Records shared with The Urbanist by Rose Terse show that in spite of not being allowed to use drones due to the surveillance ordinance, SPD was directly involved in applying for a federal grant to fund a regional drone program. During her time employed at SPD, Carrie Martin née Chitty, then the Regional Law Enforcement Homeland Security Program Manager for the SPD Metropolitan Safety Services Bureau, played a significant role in pulling together a regional drone proposal in 2020 that received money from the Homeland Security Grant Program in 2021.

Martin communicated with several local law enforcement agencies about their drone programs and convened a meeting with members of the Everett and Renton Police Departments to discuss the regional drone program and identify “a lead agency” for the grant proposal.
After the project successfully received the grant, Martin (then Chitty) explained her continuing role to Renton Police Department’s Commander Charles Karlewicz on April 1, 2021.

“The Fy21 UASI sUAS project was funded at $100,000!!! Super exciting,” Martin wrote. “I am going to be working with Deputy Chris Pelczar from KCSO TAC30 on developing the Regional deployment plan for the equipment that will be purchased with the grant funding.”
Martin is now employed as a grants administrator at KCSO, and SPD has benefited from the culmination of the regional drone project she helped bring about, often “borrowing” one of KCSO’s drones.

“It's pretty common for the SWAT team to borrow the drone for deployments where you have a barricaded armed subject,” SPD Captain James Britt told The Urbanist during a tour of the real-time crime center in 2025. “We have a great relationship with our friends over at the Sheriff's Office in their TAC 30 unit. It's common for the SWAT team to do it. It's not common beyond that.”
According to The Seattle Times , both Seattle IT and the OIG’s Inspector General for Public Safety Lisa Judge agree that the surveillance ordinance doesn’t apply when SPD calls in KCSO’s drones.
“The City can’t enforce its surveillance ordinance on other jurisdictions,” Dan Pitts, audit supervisor at the OIG, told The Urbanist .
Communities Not Cameras, a local grassroots organization that opposes surveillance, says the distinction lies in which agency is directing the activity of the drones.

“KCSO operating drones in Seattle is not, per se, a violation of that ordinance,” the group wrote to The Urbanist . “When Seattle Police direct that use, outside of exigent circumstances, they are doing so in violation of the law.”

Communities Not Cameras pointed out that in 2021, SPD submitted a Surveillance Impact Report for helicopters with infrared cameras, which was a tool they were borrowing from KCSO, and the council adopted it by ordinance.

“Drones should go through the same process. A rule that applies only to equipment SPD owns is not oversight. It is a procurement rule,” Communities Not Cameras wrote. “If borrowing exempts a tool, any technology the Council has rejected or never reviewed is one phone call away, including license plate readers, cell site simulators, and facial recognition held by neighboring agencies. Mutual aid exists for emergencies. It should not become a standing workaround for public review.”

Communities Not Cameras would like the council to amend the ordinance to state plainly that it covers any surveillance technology used at the request of, or on behalf of, a City department, regardless of who owns or operates it. They also want to include a requirement that SPD report every mutual aid request involving surveillance technology.

“The spirit, if not the letter, of the law already prohibits the department from acquiring and using drone technology through a third-party like KCSO,” Communities Not Cameras wrote. “There is just no appetite on the City’s side to enforce it.”

On the SFD side, in June, The Seattle Times reported that an AI technology had been assisting SFD 911 dispatchers since 2023 in deciding which callers would get a rapid response and which would be referred to a nurse-staffed call center in Texas. SFD has been using the AI tool, provided by the Danish company Corti, without any disclosure to the public or any evaluations of efficacy, safety, or data privacy.
Ryan Calo, a University of Washington law professor and co-director of the university’s Tech Policy Lab, shared his concerns with The Urbanist .

“People have the right to know if AI is being used to make consequential decisions such as who should be fast tracked and who should be sent on an alternative track,” Calo said. “More specifically, if you’re a person who has been sent to the nurse’s line or an alternative path because AI suggested it and you get hurt or don’t get the care you expect, you should know AI is involved. I don’t like the fact it was hidden from the public.”
Calo said he didn’t like the idea of a third party listening into 911 calls without notice.

Recent reporting from The Seattle Times uncovered a 2019 internal privacy risk analysis memo written by Ginger Armbruster, then Seattle’s chief privacy officer, which revealed concerns about data ownership and sharing, data breaches, and equity.
In September, when Kettle invited SFD leadership to a public safety committee meeting to discuss the issue, SFD Chief Harold Scoggins defended the department’s use of the Corti AI tool.
“All of our dispatchers are firefighter EMTs. They have all worked in our system,” Scoggins said.

articles.title: Nilu Jenks Wins Seattle Council Seat in Blowout
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Nilu Jenks has won a Seattle City Council seat based on the decisive 17-point lead she ran up on election night. That lead is likely to grow as more votes are counted in coming days, since last-minute votes lean progressive in Seattle. Jenks' lead held steady in Wednesday's ballot drop .

A progressive advocate, Jenks led the nonprofit FairVote Washington, which fought for the ranked-choice voting reform that is going into effect in Seattle municipal elections next year. She also ran for city council in 2023 and finished third in the primary, trailing centrist Cathy Moore and ChrisTiana ObeySumner, whom The Stranger endorsed. The Urbanist Elections Committee (on which I serve) endorsed Jenks in that 2023 race and again in 2026 .

After victory became apparent Tuesday, Jenks told The Urbanist that safety-focused designs of Aurora Avenue N and Lake City Way were among her top priorities. Aurora has a $50 million state grant earmarked for it, but state lawmakers like Seattle Rep. Julia Reed have grown impatient with the slow pace of getting the project shovel-ready.

"I would love to get the money allocated for Aurora moving and actually really get more, so that we can make Aurora a place that everybody gets to enjoy from bikers and walkers, and have good dedicated bus lanes, but also so that you can go to those businesses along there that deserve our support," Jenks said. "I also want to get similar funds for Lake City Way. It's another area where a lot of people get hit, and you know, it's not safe for pedestrians."

At an election night gathering of supporters at Mojito in North Seattle, Jenks framed her apparent victory as part of the larger battle to stop Trumpism, restore faith in American institutions, and lower the cost of living.

"As the daughter of Iranian immigrants, I know democracy is not something we can take for granted," Jenks said in her election night speech. "I grew up watching my parents lose their country, and as an Iranian American, I watch an ever-looming threat of war hang over the country my family came from while families here at home face fear, uncertainty, and rising costs. Trump's war with Iran has cost billions of dollars, with rising fuel prices adding pressure to household budgets."
With Democrats winning the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's blue wave election, pressure to end the Iran war will be ramping up.

Meanwhile, Jenks' win will shift the balance of power on Seattle City Council, growing the progressive bloc to four members. The remaining five members sometimes form a centrist bloc, although D6's Dan Strauss and D1's Rob Saka sometimes vote with progressives. Flipping the D5 seat from centrists to progressives will give Mayor Katie Wilson an easier time moving her legislation. Moreover, it will remove interim Councilmember Debora Juarez, who had been one of the mayor's harshest critics, especially on public safety issues .

Jenks has a different approach to public safety than Juarez or Moore, emphasizing the need to expand the civilian-run Community Assisted Response and Engagement (CARE) Department. When The Urbanist asked which issues she would seek to lead at council, Jenks brought up expanding CARE, tackling food deserts, and adding incentives for heat pumps as a way to shrink energy bills and the city's climate footprint.

"I am really excited to figure out food deserts and how we can solve that problem," Jenks said. "I would love to work to expand the CARE team. Get us a police chief that loves this city, and will be collaborative with an alternative response team, and ideally has worked with one before. I am excited to work on trying to figure out on-bill financing for heat pumps to stabilize our heat grid."

In winning her seat, Jenks defeated Julie Kang, an educator and former bank chair who had backing from centrist leaders in the District 5 special election. Councilmembers Bob Kettle and Maritza Rivera endorsed Kang, as did former Councilmembers Sara Nelson and Tim Burgess, who also donated to a political action committee (PAC) backing her. Current Council President Joy Hollingsworth endorsed both Jenks and Kang.

The drubbing Kang took appears as a warning sign and a repudiation for those centrists as they face their own elections next year, when all seven district-based council seats are up. D5's seat was up in an even-year special election due to Cathy Moore's decision to resign before her term was up. Jenks will assume office as soon as election results are certified later this month, rather than waiting until January, but she'll also face reelection next year.
In her speech, Jenks emphasized that she saw that District 5 residents were facing struggles and she intended to do something about it.

"I see the person who can't afford a car or the unbelievable gas prices and who relies on public transit and protected bike lanes to get around their city," Jenks said. "I see the immigrant family and the young trans person who wants what we all want: to feel safe, loved, and free to be themselves – to build a future here, and know their city will stand by them."

Another campaign focus for Jenks was food security and access, which became a hot button issue when grocery giant Kroger announced the closure of the Lake City Fred Meyer store upon which many community members had relied.

"I see the grocery store working hard for fair wages and also for accessible food in our neighborhoods. Thank you. I see the senior on a fixed income wondering whether they can afford to stay in the city they helped build as rent, housing, and property taxes keep rising," Jenks said. "I see the small business owner who has poured everything into their business and wants a safe, thriving neighborhood where they can succeed in a city that helps them instead of getting in their way, and I see the parent who wants their child to walk home safely in a city that responds to public safety with both urgency and compassion. These are the people behind this campaign, and these are the people I'm going to carry with me to City Hall."

To defeat Trump's campaigns of hate and corruption, Jenks argued Seattle must be a shining city on a hill and provide a beacon of light showing progressive leadership in big cities is able to deliver. Urbanist touchstones of high-quality transit, connected sidewalks, and abundant housing were a key part of the image Jenks invoked during her campaign, illustrating why she won The Urbanist's endorsement this year (and in 2023, for that matter). Bus improvements will be much more feasible with the passage of the Seattle Transit Measure, which ran up a huge lead in election night returns.

"That's what this moment demands of us: not that we stop being afraid, but that we refuse to let our fear decide who we become," Jenks said. "Across this country, Trump and his allies tell us our cities are broken, that the answer is more fear, more division, and more crackdowns. But Seattle is choosing another path. Once every vote counted, it's time to deliver. Our cities have to show they can govern, not someday, now. When we can't build housing, fix a sidewalk, or keep a bus stop safe, we make the argument for the people who say our cities don't work. So let's prove them wrong by making this city work for all of us."

articles.title: On the side of a bank that very nearly became apartments, a new mural confronts housing insecurity and rapid change on Capitol Hill
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: The crop of Capitol Hill murals popping up this fall includes a new work on the side of a 15th Ave E bank that would be an apartment building if the currents of redevelopment bringing change to the neighborhood twenty years ago had not been blocked by a worldwide financial meltdown.

For artist Glynn Rosenberg , her newly unveiled giant work on the north side of the street’s Key Bank is a message to Capitol Hill that the artist says explores housing insecurity and the reality “people can’t afford to live in Capitol Hill anymore” —

This mural is my love letter to my neighborhood. It is a utopian vision that reflects the past while having hope for the future. It is deeply personal to me, as I try to understand my own place in Capitol Hill. Change, progress, development – all of this moves at its own pace, determined by broader socio-economic factors – and I don’t think it can be stopped or slowed in an effort to preserve the Soul of Capitol Hill.
Key Bank says the GSBA , funding from King County, and Urban ArtWorks helped make Rosenberg’s project possible.

In 2005, Key Bank had the property lined up for a rezone approved by the city to make way for what would have been a first on the street — a 40-foot tall mixed-use apartment building. The project — with design in hand — was stopped cold by the mortgage meltdown and economic crisis that soon followed.
Today, the 1960-era bank building still stands, rising above one of the largest remaining surface parking lots on Capitol Hill.

Other mixed-use projects with dozens of new apartments have risen along the street and its current era is marked by the long wait for what will be the biggest project the strip has seen in the six-story redevelopment of the old QFC block.
Eventually, you have to think Key Bank’s part of 15th Ave E will also again be readied for a new apartments push, the old bank will need to be torn down, and Rosenberg’s art, demolished with it.

For now, the message stands and joins a flowering of new murals across Capitol Hill and a cluster of murals along 15th Ave including the Billy Davis work Sanctuary on the side of Walgreens and a Shepard Fairey design on a south-facing wall of the Hilltop Apartments .
You can find the new mural on Key Bank at 321 15th Ave E.

articles.title: Hugo House Long Story Short zine is written ‘live’ from Capitol Hill
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Think you’re a writer? Aspiring and seasoned Capitol Hill writers looking to get published can test their quick-drafting skills at Hugo House’ s upcoming community write-in, which offers participants the chance to be featured in the next issue of Long Story Short .
The volunteer-run quarterly zine is welcoming short-form submissions written on-site.

At the start of the session, organizers will unveil the issue’s secret theme and creative prompts. Attendees will then have a dedicated four-hour block to write and submit a piece of up to 500 words that aligns with the organization’s community spirit.
It sounds almost as fun as being a CHS freelancer!
Hugo House has served as a community hub for local writers and readers of all stages since 1996, offering classes, readings, and creative events.
The free event takes place Friday, November 6th, starting at 5 PM at Hugo House, located at 1634 11th Ave. Learn more at hugohouse.org .

articles.title: Say Cheese!
articles.author: Amanda Manitach
paras: There is something about this piece of cheese—waterslide transfer print on processed prepared cheese product, to be exact—that’s really doing it for me. Made by Texas-raised, Portland-based artist Ash Stone , it’s on view tonight at RailSpur as part of an exhibition called I Am Love: Rituals in Resistance . The image has been transferred onto the protective plastic sleeve sheathing a glisteny slice of orange cheese: a picture of a trailer, the kind of single- or double-wide you find plentiful in rural Texas. Surrounded by clusters of bright daylilies, an attached staircase-cum-porch leads to the closed front door, where a white-haired woman pauses, her body half-turned toward the viewer.

The Mary in Mary’s Garden is Stone’s grandmother, and the raised flowerbeds in the foreground are hers. Another piece of cheese in the show, titled Some Day , is imprinted with words that seem to have been scrawled on a Post-it-sized note: “I love you and am SO proud of you. I’m sorry it’s not the way I had hoped here—maybe it will be some day.”

Stone’s playfulness is as abundant as the faux cheese on the bottom shelf of a dairy display, and it operates on the same frequency as a Proustian madeleine. The words “say cheese” cling like an aura to the images, forcing smiles. For those of us raised in Texas (Stone included), the image of a trailer might summon a familiar, complicated nostalgia for the containers of our interior world, for home—even if that home also happened to harbor rogue rat snakes and other points of childhood pain. Using a processed food product to process an image (for the second time, after the film itself has been processed), as well as memory and experience, is a poetic device with an unexpected transformative effect. It’s anything but cheesy.

There’s a similar potency to all the gestures in Rituals in Resistance that feels disproportionate to the scale of the objects themselves, each piece or fragment of material imbued with an almost incantatory heft. What is a ritual, after all, if not the small things that make up our lives? The exhibit attends to those modest gestures, whispering their power.

Do spend some time with the cheese. Then linger with Buddy Bunting’s paintings of barbed-wire-wrapped landscapes—eerily placid and romantic depictions of high-desert correctional facilities—or Afroditi Psarra’s universe of 21st-century Greek oracles, whose magic agency has been muddied with garments embedded with AI computing. (Does the idea of that make you scream a little? Me too.) These works are provocative, full of wit, and a reminder that, even in the midst of a blue tsunami wave, our bodies remain the ultimate battleground, and patriarchy is the enemy of sovereignty. Now, here are the rest of our November recs!

November 5 Pythia Embodied at Gallery 4Culture Athens-born, Seattle-based artist Afroditi Psarra is a professor in UW’s Digital Arts and Experimental Media (DXARTS) department. Her work employs “cyber crafts” and open-source technologies to explore the subjects of our time. For Pythia Embodied (at Gallery 4Culture ) that means creating a wearable computer embedded with an AI model that allows the user to interact with artificial intelligence in a tangible way. Going deeper, the exhibition examines technology’s role in exerting control over the female and feminized body, while interrogating the way AI is increasingly viewed as a kind of magic—and a societal fix for just about everything.

Charles Mudede at Actualize AiR It’s the closing reception of Social Contract , a group exhibition curated by Actualize AiR residents Tommy Gregory and Rachael Comer. The exhibit offers works by 16 artists from across the continental United States that do not hesitate to critique our flawed government with works that are both overtly or covertly political, including some really nice pieces leveled at my freshly flipped blue home state of Texas. Stop by at 4:30 to catch The Stranger ’s own Charles Tonderai Mudede giving an informal artist lecture , “MEMORIES OF A SOFT CITY.” I highly recommend it. I highly recommend any chance to listen to Mudede talk about anything—he can imbue the way paint dries with unparalleled lyricism. And the subject of his talk is much more enthralling than paint.

Edward Wicklander and John Buck at Greg Kucera Gallery The phrase “Pissed Kitten” just rolls off the tongue, acrid and adorable. It’s the title of one of Edward Wicklander’s new pieces debuting in his solo exhibition, My Labors , at Kucera Gallery this month. The sculpture in question is a sumptuous little angry baby carved from ebonized myrtle wood and apparently endowed with actual cat whiskers? Joining Wicklander at Kucera is another artist working in wood, John Buck, whose Drawings on Wood are inspired by turn-of-the-century engravings and are made with pen and ink on jelutong, a renewable wood with a golden hue.

I Am Love: Rituals in Resistance at RailSpur Curated by tom manzanarez , I Am Love: Rituals in Resistance stems from a broader project (I Am Love) aimed at forming new connections and providing platforms for queer artists in the PNW through exhibitions, workshops, and other opportunities. It’s only continued to grow since its inception, and this month’s exhibit at RailSpur offers a window onto the region’s multidimensional, robust queer scene, featuring work by queer, trans, non-conforming, Indigenous, Black, and Brown artists (including June T. Sanders, Michael Espinoza, Ash Stone, and Teela Misa DeLeón). Objects like Espinoza’ s pairing of embroidery with i-Type Polaroids exemplify the kind of work that’s both conceptually rigorous and intimate, dexterously touching on themes of domesticity and ephemerality. (Have you ever seen a print transfer applied to a slice of processed cheese product? The poetics of the show will surprise you.)

Elsewhere during First Thursday Art Walk: J. Rinehart Gallery offers Kelda Martensen’s third solo exhibition, First Rain . Gallery No. 85 continues to showcase great printmaking, with a pleasant surprise: they’re now showing work by multimedia artist, poet, and performer Dez’Mon Omega Fair . At Shift Gallery, Cynthia Hibbard and David Traylor’s Boneyard offers a lot of bone-in work that looks beautiful. Europa Gallery’ s exhibit Mystic Journey to Nonesuch features Jade Knox , Fred Smith , Jordan Horton , Ursula Stuart , and Jd Banke (along with the usual music, food, and afters energy). Method Gallery has a solo show of work by Flora Wilds (also showing this month at The Space ; see below) that skewers commodity culture with text-on-textile art. You had me at: “if you’re obsessed with worn textiles, deconstructed fast fashion, sun-bleached sports shorts, and capital-C Criticism of late-stage capitalism…literally sewing through the cultural brainrot to interrogate all our collective anxieties.”

Elizabeth Livingston: Dark Matter at Spectrum Fine Art Beyond Pioneer Square, Spectrum has an opening tonight featuring painter of pattern Elizabeth Livingston, whose imagery borders on trompe l’oeil: immaculately rendered detail on a crumpled fabric shirt, leafy green foliage, or the flourish of a fragment of wallpaper. If you love pattern for pattern’s sake, you’ll eat this lush visual imagery up.

November 6 An Indigenous Present a t Frye Art Museum Tapestries made of AstroTurf and buckskin, blankets woven from ink and tape, a Cree prayer rendered in blood-red acrylic and powdery pastel: One of the year’s most anticipated shows (mine at least) opens this month at the Frye. An Indigenous Present is a traveling exhibition co-organized by the renowned artist Jeffrey Gibson and independent curator Jenelle Porter that includes major works and commissions by 15 Indigenous artists, spanning 100 years of Indigenous art. The exhibition embodies a shift in how Indigenous identity is represented within institutional spaces, as artists move beyond redefining their place within these institutions to actively defying the colonial constraints and expectations they have imposed for centuries. Alongside An Indigenous Present , the museum has mounted My Body Is a Basket , featuring work by three Indigenous Pacific Northwest artists—Brenda Mallory, Danielle Morsette, and Sara Siestreem—who push traditional basket weaving into unexpected conceptual and metaphorical territory.

Tess Michalik: Rococo Puffs at Dirkse/Prim In conversation with the show at Spectrum this month, Tess Michalik’s Rococo Puffs explores the exuberant impermanence of floral life through compositions inspired by the 17th- and 18th-century European textile designs found in brocade silk and woven tapestries. The unbridled decadence of rococo design, with all the gushing blossoms and impending rot serves a memento mori sensibility that’s as delicious as Michalik’s use of thick, sculptural impasto oil paint, slathered on with palette knife.

November 13 The Mothership at Behnke Family Galler y at Cornish The Mothership Photography Collective brings together a powerhouse of 13 Seattle-area photographers who also happen to be mothers. The exhibition, featuring more than 50 works, is taking on the subject of motherhood and how it intersects with creative practice and artistic identity, including both the good and bad (combating the persistent marginalization of mothers in the art world).

November 14 Form Over Function: Held Together at Seattle Art Source The third annual group exhibition at Seattle Art Source, Held Together, is a showcase of some of the city’s most most exciting figurative artists, co-curated by artist Seth Sexton , featuring work by Kelly Bjork , Michael Doyle , Amy Erickson , Becca Fuhrman , Nahom Ghirmay , Barry Johnson , Kade Marsili , Amy Scherer , Zachary Schomburg , and Kimberly Trowbridge . Note: there’s an artist talk on November 10 that should be loaded with meaty stuff.

At studio e , catch dual solo shows Warren Dykeman: GLYPH & GROUND and Buddy Bunting: High Desert Landscapes, 2024-26 . Bunting’s paintings of correctional and industrial facilities in the Mojave Desert are unusual subjects; he’s been documenting in nearly 30 years of field research across California prompted by the incarceration of Bunting’s childhood friend. The paintings are small (each less than 14 x 18 inches) and their

November 14 & 15 Light the Forest at Pilchuck Glass School About an hour’s drive north of Seattle, there’s a magical place called Pilchuck Glass School where the world’s top glass artists convene throughout the year to whip miraculous glass art into existence in boiling hot shops and less-hot cold shops. The campus is a work of art in its own right: It spreads out like a 1970s hobbit fantasy complete with forests threaded with secret paths, stained-glass follies, and treehouses where acolytes retire to revel at the end of a long day’s work. The school isn’t typically accessible to the public, which makes the annual Light the Forest even more special. The event—a self-guided walking tour—unfolds on two dusky November nights, during which the already-ensorcelling Pilchuck campus transforms into an immersive light installation ablaze with neon. This year’s artists are Seattle-based glass baddies MiNHi England and John Sharvin (who both appeared on season 3 of Blown Away ). Did I mention it’s magical? I can’t overemphasize how utterly enchanted it is. This year, they’re also offering day-of workshops, so you can walk away with your very own neon creation or hand-blown ornaments.

November 15 SUNDAY SERVICE at Kenyon Hall If you’re a recovering church kid like me, eternally grappling with a love-hate longing-loathing for congregation life of yore, or if you’re a fan of Pastor Kaleb’s Easter Service, or if you just want to participate in a non-run-of-the-mill art happening, then get thine divine ass to SUNDAY SERVICE . The event is led by the Good Rev. N.M. Langston, a.k.a. Nathan Langston, engineer, musician, and director of the expansive global art game TELEPHONE (which exhibited at Base Camp 2 last year). Langston is blessed with an exquisite, honey-tongued gift of gab, and he’s been letting it loose at this semiregular, secular gathering of congregants playing “make-believe church revival.” It’s got the trappings of real church (non-hymnal hymns!), but the only religion being practiced here is art, music, film, poetry, and community vibes. Special guests and speakers at this month’s service include Israel Nebeker of Blind Pilot; artist, writer, activist, and educator Amber Flame; writer, publisher, and former EIC of The Stranger , Christopher Frizzelle; and musician, producer, and music supervisor Kaylee Cole. Tickets start at $15 and all profits go to the West Seattle Food Bank for assembling weekend meal kits for children in need. Now, that’s doing the lord’s work.

November 19 Fade Into You at The Space Columbia City art walk kicks off with Fade Into You at The Space , an exhibit hosted by Disposable Parts featuring a group of artists who are doing radical things with textiles, trash, and other detritus: Janelle R. Abbott , Dagny Rayn Chika , Sam Guccione , Cameron Kester , Cathy McClure , Morgan Rosskopf , and Flora Wilds .

November 27 Cristina Martinez at Hometeam Gallery One of our city’s most prolific and ascendant artists, Cristina Martinez creates figurative imagery that taps into something both emotional and sensual with its lavish saturated color and elongated, monumental bodies that take up space. (Her recent mural, A Soft Place to Land , located along Occidental Promenade near Lumen Field measures 150 feet wide and covers 9,000 square feet.) Hometeam is hosting a special opening on Black Friday (the show will run through the December art walk as well), so mark your calendars if you’re looking to score some art for the holidays.

Ongoing (Through December 19) Hyunjeong Lim: Archive of the Mind at Winston Wächter Fine Art Hyunjeong Lim is our November cover artist! Drawing from traditional Korean landscape and Renaissance painting, Lim’s landscapes have an almost fairytale-like quality, and they’re packed with so much detail, you can’t help but fall in and get lost. Her latest body of work at Winston Wächter is embroidered with scenes from the American West and Pacific Northwest: lakes, canyons, and lost highways winding around craggy outcroppings and islands sprouting like mushrooms from the sea. Look closer and you’ll find the terrain populated by tiny, quizzical blob people, unhinged grotesqueries plucked straight from Hieronymus Bosch, and even art history Easter eggs. For Lim, landscape is more than a pretty picture of a place: It serves as a container where lived experience tangles with imagination and memory. Because of that, her places feel uncannily placeless, but also like everywhere you’ve ever been. We love them because we have been there—if not in the flesh, then in dream.

articles.title: Democrats on Course for Supermajority in Washington State House, Election Night Results Show
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Democrats scored victories up and down the ballot across the country Tuesday night, and the picture in Washington state was no different. Election night returns, when about half of ballots are counted in Washington's vote-by-mail elections, indicated Democrats are likely on course to a two-thirds supermajority in the state House.

The Urbanist laid out the path to a Democratic supermajority in our post-primary analysis , and basically everything that could break their way did. Legislative District 17 and 18 in Clark County swung from Republicans to Democrats, as did LD14 in the Yakima Valley, clearing indicating a shift among Latino voters and high turnout in the Democratic base.

The last Republican holdout in Kitsap County's Legislative District 26 is no more, giving Democrats another pickup. Urbanist-endorsed Democrat Renee Hernandez Greenfield is up nearly 10 points over Republican Katy Cornell, who was hoping to pick up the baton from retiring Rep. Michelle Caldier.

The Democratic gains build on a decade of steady progress expanding their legislative margins. After the 2024 election, Democrats surpassed 60% in both chambers, but most supermajority advantages, like the possibility of passing amendments to the state constitution, kick in at the two-thirds mark.

Even races not fully on the radar as realistic pickup opportunities, like LD12 Position 1 and the LD35 senate race saw Democrats in the lead on election night. These largely rural districts have long been Republican strongholds.

In the 25th LD, school board director David Berg is leading Republican Rep. Michael Keaton by 1.6 points. The 25th represents the last district in the Seattle-Tacoma metropolitan area still held by Republicans after a decade of steady losses. Republican seatmate Cyndy Jacobsen is grasping to a razor-thin 109-vote lead over Democratic challenger Jenn Marie Strickling.

In the 35th, Democrat Carolina Mejia has a three-point lead over incumbent Republican Drew MacEwan. Down ballot, the Republican incumbents Dan Griffey and Travis Couture hold slim leads under one point. Democrat Jim Pierson is just 212 votes behind Griffey with tons of votes still to count.

In the 12th, Democrat challenger Stacy Willoughby is up three points over incumbent Republican Rep. Brian Burnett. The district covers Chelan County and crosses the Cascades into the eastern reaches of King and Snohomish counties. Republican seatmate Rep. Mike Steele is comfortably ahead, meanwhile, suggesting Burnett's profile – a Trump-endorsed former Chelan County sheriff is particularly odious to voters right now.

In the 39th, Republicans are also clinging to thin leads. On election night, Democrat Ida Keeley trailed Republican Steve Ewing by just 282 votes, with both vying to replace Rep. Caroline Eslick, who retired. GOP incumbent Sam Low had a larger five-point lead over Democrat Kathryn Lewandowsky in the Position 1 race. In 2024, a Democrat didn't even make it though the primary to face Low, and no Democrat ran against Eslick at all.

While likely on the path to a two-thirds majority in the state House, Democrats were not able to make quite the same gains in the state Senate, where only half of the seats are up in any given year. In a stroke of bad luck for Democrats, several Republican-held seats in more swing-y districts were not up this year, including LD14, LD17, LD25, and LD39. However, it could be tough sledding for those Republican incumbents in 2028 unless the state's political mood shifts significantly.

If election night leads hold, the Democrats' advantage in the state house will grow from 59-39 to 66-32, just across the two-thirds threshold. Pulling ahead in some or all of the close races in LD25-2, LD35-1, LD35-2, and LD39-2 would expand that supermajority.
Some efforts from conservative megadonors to defend centrist Democrats from progressive challenges also fell flat.

In the 48th LD, Redmond Councilmember Jessica Forsythe (who is Urbanist-endorsed) is leading incumbent State Rep. Amy Walen by five points in election night results, despite more than a $1 million in outside spending. Microsoft-funded Washington Need to Compete political action committee (PAC) led the way investing $700,000 in the race. Walen once one of the few Democrats to vote against the millionaires tax, drawing ire from the progressive wing of the party. Forsythe saw a fair share of spending on her own behalf, with the state-employee funded New Direction PAC putting up more than $300,000 against Walen on top of $260,000 to promote Forsythe.

In the 29th LD, Democratic Rep. Melanie Morgan looks like she will lose to progressive, Urbanist-endorser challenger Krista Perez, after trailing by three points on election night. Morgan voted against the millionaires tax, breaking with her caucus.

Republicans also launched a frontal assault on the millionaires tax via statewide Initiative Measure No. 645, aiming to repeal the tax and blow a major hole in the state budget. That measure was resoundingly defeated, falling just short of 42% of the vote on election night. Democrats seeking to triangulate in opposing the millionaires tax seem to have made a miscalculation; they would have been more popular if they voted for it.

Republican efforts to force conservative judges onto the state Supreme Court also appears to have fizzled. The one exception is that Ian Birk (Urbanist-endorsed) is trailing Republican-backed Sean O'Donnell by two points, and will need to close the gap in later returns to survive. A Supreme Court takeover would have offered another route for conservatives to block the millionaires tax or other similar progressive revenue sources, but it doesn't look like the scheme worked.

Let's Go Washington, a PAC led by hedge fund multimillionaire Brian Heywood, ran the repeal measure along with two initiatives targeting trans rights . Initiative Measure 1 (which forces schools to potentially out queer kids to unsupportive parents) looks like it will fail, as it's down five points. However, Initiative Measure 638, which seeks to block trans girls from participating in school athletics, looks like it will pass, as it has 56% of the vote so far.
The setback on trans rights was one of the few blemishes on an otherwise triumphant night for progressives.
Correction : The initial version of this article incorrectly listed Amy Walen as a state senator, rather than a state representative.

articles.title: Transit Measures Headed to Victory in Seattle, Pierce County
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Bus riders in Seattle and Pierce County are poised to see increased transit service in the wake of successful funding measures, with early returns showing strong voter support in both jurisdictions. Seattle's transit measure, which renews an existing sales tax measure supplementing King County Metro service, is ahead with 72.5% of the vote, while the funding measure for Pierce Transit is leading with a very respectable 57.7%.

Both propositions will bump up the local sales tax rate by 0.3% to fund bus service, with Seattle's measure set to enable nearly 100,000 more King County Metro bus trips every year on top of the 180,000 currently provided. It would also continue funding existing transit-related programs, including streetcar service and a major expansion of the number of subsidized ORCA transit cards provided by the City of Seattle.

Pierce Transit's measure will bump up service by nearly 50% compared to the levels seen today, expanding hours of operation and frequency across the entire network along with adding four brand new bus routes. It will also enable the agency to eliminate fares for seniors, building on the existing statewide free youth fare program.

A success at the ballot box in Seattle was all but assured, given the track record of the existing Seattle Transit Measure, which has been in place since 2014. The 2020 renewal passed with 80.3% of the vote , a nationwide record for a transit funding measure that has still never been surpassed. But for Pierce Transit, things were much less less certain in terms of going to the voters for more funding.

Serving Tacoma, Puyallup, Lakewood, University Place, Spanaway and Gig Harbor, Pierce Transit has been operating at a lower funding level than other peer agencies across the region for decades. A pair of defeated measures in 2011 and 2012 led to substantial service cuts and a contraction of the agency's total service area.
Those defeats ultimately led to a reluctance to head back to the ballot that was overcome this year, prompted by strong polling and high expected turnout during a midterm election.

The results are a major source of vindication for Pierce County's elected transit champions, including Tacoma City Councilmember Kristina Walker and Pierce County Executive Ryan Mello. Mello has been clear about the need to expand transit access in Pierce County since being elected in 2024, taking over after eight years of Republican leadership.

"For me, what it means is finally having a transit system that will connect more people to opportunity, to run their life and the essentials of their life," Mello told The Urbanist in an interview Wednesday morning. "So many of the things that I'm working on: connecting people to opportunity, connecting people to jobs, getting to school, after school programs to keep people safe, connecting vulnerable community members to healthcare and other services — the common barrier, time and time again, is transportation."

The 47% increase in service will be phased in by the early 2030s, ending the era of the hourly bus on the Pierce Transit network. The number of bus routes that operate every 30 minutes will jump from 18 to 24, with seven routes going to 15-20 minutes – frequency boosts that will represent a game changer for access across Pierce County.
Mello told The Urbanist that the 15-point margin on election night was a pleasant surprise.

"I was prepared for a much closer margin. I know we ran a really good campaign. I know we had a really clear message about what we were going to deliver, but you know, it's a tax measure in this economy, in this significant sense of uncertainty, there was a lot of concern about: would voters still be willing to invest in themselves and our community in this way," Mello said. "But they they surely see the value of making sure that more people can get access to opportunity, and I'm so proud of my neighbors for seeing the power of transit to connect more people to opportunity."

The passage of the Seattle Transit Measure Tuesday night notches a major win for Mayor Katie Wilson, who proposed doubling the existing 0.15% sales tax rate to 0.3%. Though that move was met with a hand-wringing over cost impacts that hasn't been seen with other sales tax bumps – including a 0.1% increase for public safety investments approved last year by her predecessor Bruce Harrell – Wilson made the case that increasing access to transit will outweigh the sales tax bump when it comes to the affordability impact for city residents.

"I just want to drive home the point that this is an affordability measure, and when gas is $6 a gallon, when the price of car ownership has never been higher, this measure – fast, frequent bus service, is going to allow more people, more households around our city, to get around on a most affordable mode of transportation," Wilson told transit supporters gathered at a Proposition 1 party in Pioneer Square. "And we are not going to stop until Seattle's transit system is irresistibly good."

Wilson was clearly in her element Tuesday night, with the win representing a full circle moment. Prior to being elected Mayor, Wilson led the Transit Riders Union, an organization that got its start advocating for transit funding in Seattle. In 2011, Wilson helped to launch the Save Our Metro! campaign to push against pending Metro service cuts stemming from the Great Recession. After those cuts were averted with a $20 car tab fee approved by the King County Council, the group pivoted to other transit fights including a push for a countywide low-income fare program.

"Seattle is not just a great transit city; it is the great transit city. And tonight shows us that that is still true," Wilson said. "This year has been a banner year for public transit in our city and our region. We've had some of the highest rebounding ridership in the country. We have opened up some of the most ambitious capital infrastructure anywhere in the U.S. We now have a light rail station that has the highest ridership of any light rail system in the whole entire country."
With the 2 Line now crossing Lake Washington, Sound Transit has surpassed 160,000 daily boardings, making it the most-ridden light rail system in the country.

With Seattle largely maxing out its transit funding capabilities with this renewal, attention is set to turn to King County Metro, which will be buoyed by this funding but still in need of a more sustainable long-term funding source to keep the agency stable. The millionaire's tax voters also upheld Tuesday means even less sales tax funding will be flowing into Metro's coffers at the end of this decade than had been expected, due to planned sales tax exemptions. King County Executive Girmay Zahilay will have to start to address a looming budget shortfall by next year's biennial budget.

"Seattle and King County residents deserve safe, affordable, and world-class transit. Renewing the Seattle Transit Measure reflects voters’ commitment to stronger, more connected communities by adding thousands of hours of Metro service, expanding early morning and late-night service, and providing free transit passes to more students, working families, and low-income residents," Zahilay said in a statement after the results dropped. "This historic investment will help Metro reach more communities and ensure more people have a sustainable, affordable, reliable way to get where they need to go."

The transit funding push across the region isn't even over. On Wednesday night, the Everett City Council will decide whether to give the green light for Community Transit to annex Everett Transit , trading away the city-specific 0.6% sales tax rate for Community Transit's 1.2%. That move will come with a 50% increase in transit service within the city by 2031, and transit connections that simply can't exist with Snohomish County's largest city maintaining a completely separate transit agency.
Wednesday's vote will be followed by a vote of the Community Transit board on Thursday.

Thanks to a 2025 change in state law, Everett Transit's annexation will be able to happen without the voters directly weighing in. But the move represents a bold swing by three-term Everett Mayor Cassie Franklin, who has been making the case that the city can't grow sustainably without making substantial investments in transit.

Earlier this year, voters in and around Spokane also signed onto a 0.2% sales tax measure that will allow Spokane Transit to maintain existing service and grow in the future. Clearly, the momentum is on the side of transit expansion in 2026 in Washington State.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: ORCA Survey
articles.author: Mike Orr
paras: The ORCA consortium has a survey asking users about their experiences using ORCA cards and the fare payment system. The survey is open until mid November. The Friday Roundtable column is for short, light, interactive topics, so this is an opportunity to ask readers the same question: how is your experience using ORCA cards and the fare payment system in general?

There are several aspects to consider. There’s tapping an ORCA card, or using a credit card with the new open-payment system for credit cards. Using the readers may be better or worse on Link, regular buses, RapidRide, or Sounder. There’s obtaining the card and refilling it, at a ticket vending machine (TVM), at the MyORCA.com website, or getting a card mailed to you. There’s customer service offices. There’s the fare structure, and free transfers. There’s the times you have to explain the system to visitors or occasional riders at the platform or bus stop when it’s not obvious to them. And probably many other things.
My two biggest issues with ORCA are the time it takes to register a tap, and paying for part of a pass with an e-purse.

When you hold an ORCA card to a reader, the second-generation system takes twice as long to register a tap than the previous system did. So on buses I either have to hold up the line behind me, or tap and leave and assume it will either beep while I’m walking away or it won’t beep and I’ll get a free ride.

The second issue is when you want to split a pass cost between e-purse and a credit card. I switched to e-purse during the pandemic, and back to a pass this year. In the past at TVMs I’ve been able to use the $60 e-purse value for partial payment for the $108 pass, and pay the rest by credit card. I’d then have to do a second credit-card payment to put $10 back into the e-purse for occasional surcharges, because it had no option to take just $50 out of the e-purse and leave the other $10.

This year when I went back to using passes, the TVM wouldn’t even do that. The e-purse option was disabled, so the only choices were credit card or cash. That’s presumably because the e-purse value wasn’t enough for the entire pass. I didn’t want to leave $60 in the e-purse unused forever, so I went to Metro’s customer service office to make the kind of payment split I wanted. It would be nice if the TVMs could do this.

articles.title: Sound Transit Pilots Updated Pet Policy
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: Sound Transit is piloting an updated pet policy on its buses and trains between now and Spring 2027. During the pilot, pet dogs will be permitted on board if they are leashed, well-behaved, and controlled by their handler. All other pets must remain in an enclosed carrier. As always, service animals are permitted in compliance with the ADA.

Prior to the pilot, dogs and other pets were only allowed on Sound Transit buses and trains in a carrier. In July 2025, the Sound Transit Board approved Motion No. M2025-34 , directing the agency to consider updating the rules to allow leashed dogs. This motion was motivated by the opening of Marymoor Village station as part of the Downtown Redmond Link Extension in May 2025. Marymoor Village station is next to Marymoor Park, a 640-arce park which includes a 40-arce off-leash dog area.

Will this pilot impact the passenger experience on Sound Transit? Probably not. In a presentation to the Executive Committee before the motion was approved, then-Acting Executive Director of Security & Fare Engagement Brian de Place acknowledged that passengers already take leashed dogs on Sound Transit buses and trains. While doing so did violate the rules, de Place noted “if the dog is leashed and generally under control, security will not engage with that passenger unless there is an actual disturbance”. In the year prior to this meeting, Sound Transit security only received 8 calls about pets.
There are few other notes pet owners should be aware of before bringing their leashed dogs onboard:
If you encounter an aggressive animal or other issues, call or text Sound Transit security: (206) 398-5268. In an emergency, call 911.

articles.title: The 38 Best Restaurants in Seattle
articles.author: <name>Sophie Grossman</name>
paras: “Where should I eat in Seattle?” Whether you’re a first-time visitor or a lifer, that question is seemingly simple but the answers are infinitely complex. Some of the main factors to consider are the type of food, price point, neighborhood, and occasion. That’s why Eater’s map of the 38 best restaurants in Seattle exists. This curated list of suggestions attempts to capture the diversity of the food scene in the Seattle metro area, from English pubs serving cumin-y lamb neck meat pies to Indian street food takeout spots, from classic French bistros to modern sushi bars, and so much more. Every place on the list has been open for at least six months, proving its merit.

Like many menus, this map updates every quarter — removal from the Eater 38 doesn’t mean a restaurant isn’t still awesome and won’t return in the future. New to the map as of October 2026: tamale and specialty coffee haven Cafetal Quilombo Cafe, Thai dumpling hotspot E-Jae Pak Mor, and Dim Sum King, which reigns supreme in counter-service dim sum.

A note on pricing: $ means entrees are mostly under $15; $$ means entrees are mostly under $25; $$$ means entrees are priced under $35; and $$$$ means entrees are more expensive than that, or it is primarily a tasting menu restaurant. (Prices are always subject to change.)

paras: The University District is frequently (and wrongly) written off as a place only college kids would want to eat; the story usually goes that it’s rife with sketchy lunch counters, nondescript multinational fast food chains, and an overabundance of boba tea joints. But the truth is that the U District is one of the city’s essential dining destinations, with a dizzying array of global cuisines concentrated on its main street, University Way (confusingly known as the Ave).

There’s Korean food, regional Chinese specialties, Indian groceries, Vietnamese kitchens, falafel windows, and more on nearly every block. And practically everything is both affordable and genuinely good, so figuring out where to eat in this neighborhood is more a matter of grappling with the paradox of choice than anything else. articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Ballard
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?
